https://www.jpost.com/opinion/article-90.text: I'm standing with my husband at the port in Thessaloniki, a vital commercial hub on the Aegean Sea connecting Southern Europe with the Balkans.I'm thinking of the Jewish stevedores who once worked these docks, and of those who later made aliyah and helped haul cargo on the waterfronts of pre-state Israel. Men from this community were also among the Sonderkommando prisoners who revolted at Auschwitz-Birkenau and destroyed crematorium IV.When a proposed flight of two hours and 20 minutes appeared on my computer screen from Sun d'Or, El Al's subsidiary, I booked tickets for my husband and me.I had long wanted to visit the city where the port once closed on Shabbat, and where Jews were both longshoremen and leaders in commercial development. I didn't know much more than that.I was about to learn a great deal.First, the name.The Jewish community used a shortened form, spelled either Salonika or Salonica, and referred to this pretty city on the sea as “La Madre de Israel,” the Mother of Israel, and the “Jerusalem of the Balkans.”Thessaloniki is the older name, and it commemorates a woman. Thessalonike was the half-sister of Alexander the Great and the wife of Cassander, who founded the city in 315 BCE. According to Greek legend, after Thessalonike's death she became a mermaid who appeared before passing ships and inquired if her brother Alexander was still alive. The sailors had to answer, “He lives and reigns and conquers the world.” If they answered incorrectly, she would metamorphose into a monster and sink their ships.There are legends, too, that Jews arrived with King Cassander, but no one knows exactly when Jews first settled in Thessaloniki. The city's Jewish Museum describes an ancient Romaniote community, traditionally dated to around 140 BCE. They spoke a Jewish form of Greek known as Yevanic. They were joined many centuries later by the more than 20,000 Jews expelled from Spain in 1492, and from Portugal several years later.Spain's loss was Thessaloniki's gain. The intellectual and commercial talents of the Golden Age of Spanish Jewry enhanced the seaside city. The newcomers prospered in business, printing, scholarship, and the arts.Eventually, Jews made up half the population, and Ladino became one of the city's principal languages. The port, which the Jews expanded and where they served as merchants, brokers, and longshoremen, naturally closed on Shabbat.As a capellophile, I shopped in a hat shop called Stamion, “established 1914.” I learned that the proprietors weren't Jewish, but that previous generations of the family had spoken fluent Ladino because so many of their hat-wearing customers were Jews.In 1917, a cooking fire spread and ravaged Thessaloniki. More than 70,000 people were left homeless, approximately 52,000 of them Sephardi Jews. Many Jews left for Paris, New York, and pre-state Israel. Experienced Jewish longshoremen from Salonika played an important role in developing the ports of Haifa and Tel Aviv.The day of rest was changed to Sunday. The Jewish Museum documents the rise and fall of one of the world's outstanding Jewish communities, as well as today's Jewish community.The museum's ground floor is surprisingly dominated by recovered tombstones.Until December 1942, an enormous Jewish cemetery containing hundreds of thousands of graves occupied the land on which the city's Aristotle University now stands. Some graves dated back to the 15th century. Empowered by the Nazis who conquered Greece, municipal workers arrived with pickaxes to topple the graves and take the land. Marble was used for a swimming pool for German soldiers, for church renovations, for pavements, and for private courtyards. The Hebrew lettering was scratched away, or the stones were turned over.Recovering the gravestones remains an ongoing process.This reminded me, of course, of the devastation of the Jewish cemetery on the Mount of Olives between 1948 and 1967. I have often visited the grave of Hadassah founder Henrietta Szold, who died in 1945. Her headstone was used as road pavement. After the Six Day War, the cemetery caretaker found it and returned it to her grave.Thessaloniki's Jews were forced to remove bodies from gas chambers at AuschwitzAT THE Monastirioton Synagogue, which survived because it was used by the Red Cross during the German occupation, we were privileged to hear Elia Matalon, a retired surveyor and civil engineer, recount the history of the community through both public events and the experiences of his family and those of his wife, fellow guide Hella Kunio Matalon.Long ago, on a tour of Auschwitz-Birkenau, I heard that Jews from Thessaloniki, known for their physical strength as longshoremen, were forced into the Sonderkommando units. These prisoners had the horrifying task of removing bodies from the gas chambers and bringing them to the crematoria.I knew about the mighty Jewish boxer Salamo Arouch, a longshoreman about whom a movie was made. I had never understood how an entire community of more than 50,000 people, including so many tough, experienced port workers, could have been transported to Auschwitz with so little organized resistance.Matalon explained how thoroughly the community had been deceived.Hard as it is to imagine in today's world of instant communication, the Jews of Thessaloniki didn't know about the concentration camps and death camps of Poland. Using a modified strategy, the Germans initially avoided sealing them inside the kind of starvation ghettos found in Eastern Europe. The boundaries of the ghettos were porous. Matalon's mother-in-law, then a schoolgirl, would leave in the afternoon to meet her non-Jewish Greek friends and return at night.The Germans promoted the fiction of a “New Europe” in which unemployed and hungry Jews would supposedly find jobs, education, and abundant food in Poland.Rabbi Zvi Koretz, the city's chief rabbi, remains a contentious figure. He had been arrested by the Germans and imprisoned near Vienna before being returned to Thessaloniki. Matalon believes that Koretz came back a manipulated and manipulative man.Koretz preached at the many city synagogues that the Jews should embrace relocation. The community was led to believe that families would travel together by train and be resettled together. Instead, they were forced into cattle cars, and it was too late to turn around.More than 53,000 members of the Jewish community, out of a population of 56,000, were murdered.Matalon's mother-in-law came from a large family that had experienced an earlier confrontation with the Nazis. That experience led some family members to suspect that the promises of resettlement were a ruse. Even so, of the 23 members of the extended family, only his future in-laws and the daughter who would become his wife went into hiding. The others were murdered at Auschwitz.“They felt it inconceivable that their entire community could be destroyed,” Matalon told us.His own family survived because Righteous Gentiles hid them in Albania.Thessaloniki has begun acknowledging the Jews who contributed to its historyLater, walking through the port, my husband mused that perhaps we should not have come. Too many residents of Thessaloniki had been complicit. Too many had taken possession of Jewish apartments, shops, furnishings, and property. We had not understood the full scope of the tragedy that had befallen this magnificent Jewish community.Last year, we visited Chalkida, another Greek city, where non-Jewish residents helped save their Jews.But then, we thought, staying away would leave its Jewish history even more invisible. How will we know if we don't come and see?In more recent years, Thessaloniki has begun acknowledging the Jews who contributed so much. Holocaust memorials have been erected, and signs identify Jewish contributions to the city's commercial and architectural life.Greece is making a huge investment in Israeli defensive technology. Our Uber driver praised Israel for objecting to the sale of advanced fighter planes to Turkey.At the Monastirioton Synagogue, we heard Elia Matalon sing the popular Ladino song “Adio Kerida,” Goodbye, Beloved. It's a haunting song of wounded love and departure. Matalon told us that Jews sang it to their city as they stood beside the railway tracks.The beloved had betrayed them.“I'll go find another love. I hope there is a real love there,” the song proposes.An estimated 55,000 descendants of Greek Jews live in Israel today, many of them with roots in Thessaloniki.■The writer is the Israel director of public relations at Hadassah, the Women's Zionist Organization of America. Her latest book is A Daughter of Many Mothers, cowritten with Holocaust survivor and premier English-language witness Rena Quint.

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-plans-anti.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5LhC0 Germany reportedly plans a new shield against sabotage at critical sites Image: Ardan Fuessmann/IMAGO Advertisement Germany is planning a comprehensive protective shield to prevent attacks like the failed assault on Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sunday. On August 4, several small drones targeted Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, with one hitting a parked plane, while another is thought to have struck an inbound cargo jet. German intelligence agencies blamed Russia for the incident, which Moscow has denied. Leipzig-Halle Airport is a major cargo hub used to fly weapons and supplies toward Ukraine Image: Daniel Kessler/imageBROKER/picture alliance What did Dobrindt say about the shield? Dobrindt told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that Russia's hybrid attacks are now a "daily" reality, adding: "These attacks will increase, but we can defend ourselves and protect ourselves." The newspaper cited information from the Interior Ministry showing the government plans to expand the federal police's mobile drone-defense units. The measures include vehicles and helicopters that can be quickly deployed to protect airspace over key cities like Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin to counter drone attacks. Bild said the shield would not only intercept drones, but could also defuse drone bombs and other explosive devices. The newspaper described how a change in the law would allow critical infrastructure operators — including water, power and defense companies — to detect and defend against drone sabotage. Jammers flood drones with radio noise, so its pilot can no longer steer it Image: Michael Bihlmayer/Bihlmayerfotografie/IMAGO Russia's Lavrov accuses Merz of wanting war On Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed the German accusations levelled against Russia were "by ​and ​large, the ​start of ‌a real war." He reiterated Russia's denial of any involvement with the Leipzig drone attack and criticized German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for wanting to boost the country's military capability in response to hybrid threats. "All ‌these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in ‌Europe once again — they are ‌being ​put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov told Russian state-run TV channel Vesti. He also criticized Germany's closure of Russian House cultural center in berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn. Putin denies Russian involvement in Leipzig drone attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video New tech planned to boost cyber security Bild also described how a national protective cyber shield would be set up to detect and intercept hacking attacks. The measure comes amid hundreds of cyberattacks on government departments, infrastructure and companies each day, many of them blamed on Russia, other states and criminal gangs. The newspaper said the government ⁠also wants to increase the use of AI, biometric facial recognition ⁠and video surveillance, especially at transport hubs, to identify suspected attackers before they carry out attacks. Over 1,000 drone sightings in 2025 The head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch, told Bild in December that more than a thousand suspicious drone flights were recorded over Germany last year. These incidents mostly targeted military sites, airports, ports and defense firms and were treated as surveillance or harassment, rather than attacks. Leipzig airport has been targeted by sabotage before. In July 2024, a suspected Russian incendiary parcel caught fire at the airport's DHL hub. The cargo hub is also utilized by the Ukrainian military and NATO to airlift arms for use in the Ukrainian defense against Russia's invasion . https://www.express.co.uk/news/politics/.text: Home News Politics Nigel Farage EXCLUSIVE: Migrants, Burnham and Brexit Nigel Farage has declared that Britain will never "vote to rejoin" the EU as fears intensify that Andy Burnham is plotting a second referendum . The Reform UK leader accused the Prime Minister of having a “completely outdated view of the world” where he regards the EU as a “big, lovely, friendly, cuddly club”. And Mr Farage warned pressure from Labour’s traditional heartlands in the North will prevent him from leading Britain straight back into the bloc. He told the Sunday Express leaving in 2016 was the "hard thing to do", adding the country will never "vote to rejoin". Large swathes of Northern England and the Midlands abandoned the party after Brexit , first turning to Boris Johnson in 2019 and then voting Reform in the 2026 local elections. Mr Farage told the Express: “Blair wanted to join the euro, but he was forced into promising a referendum. I suspect the pressure on Burnham from the North would mean he'd have to put it as a referendum. “I think Burnham will be forced into promising a referendum, to which I would say, why on earth would you want to put the country through all that again? I mean, Burnham says: 'Look, I'm a nice, lovely, cuddly guy. I want to unite the country.' I can't think of anything that would, frankly, that would divide it as much as this. “Voting to Leave was the hard thing to do. Not rejoining will be an easy thing to do. Why would you join this club? Look at the obstacles, look at the barriers, look at the costs, what it would mean. We would never vote to rejoin.” EU leaders gathering in Brussels admitted they would welcome Britain back with open arms – for a price. Mr Farage claimed this would be £42billion a year. Czech prime minister Andrej Babis was accused of saying “the quiet bit out loud” when he said of Britain rejoining: “Of course, we need more money.” And the Netherlands’ prime minister Rob Jetten said: “In the end, it’s up to the British people to decide what the relationship looks like.” Nigel Farage speaks to Essex county councillors (Image: Steve Finn Photography) Bulgaria’s prime minister Rumen Radev even said the UK can return but “must learn its lesson”. Slovenia’s prime minister Janez Jansa said: “The UK leaving was one of the biggest catastrophes for the EU in the entire time of its existence.” In Sunderland, which voted to Leave the EU, Reform claimed 58 of the 75 council seats up for grabs. And in Wigan, Mr Farage’s party won all but one of the 25 seats on offer. In the Prime Minister’s constituency of Makerfield, 65% voted to leave. Labour also lost control of Barnsley for the first time in the council’s 52-year history. The South Yorkshire town overwhelmingly voted to Leave. But Mr Burnham has said it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to get a better deal with Brussels, claiming it would boost economic growth and tackle illegal immigration. The Labour leader declared he will use an EU summit next month as a launchpad for restoring ties. He confirmed the two sides are looking at a deal to ease the movement of food and drink across borders, as well as a controversial youth “free movement” scheme. Hinting he wants to go even further, Mr Burnham told MPs there was an “opportunity” to improve ties because the “status quo is not good enough” for Britain. The Prime Minister also stressed that he wanted the meeting to be the start of a “serious dialogue” about the future relationship. Nigel Farage meets private security guards in Chelmsford (Image: Steve Finn Photography) But Mr Farage told the Express: “The Prime Minister is stuck with a completely outdated view of the world. That somehow Europe is this big, lovely, friendly, cuddly club, and it's all great, we'll all be friends. Well, that was then. Now is very different. “I'd love to see him sitting down with the AfD. I'd love to see him sitting down with President Le Pen. What kind of Europe does he think it is? “He seems to be trying to coalesce a vote from Greens and Lib Dems who have this same outdated idea of Europe. Some are genuine globalists. Some don't believe in national countries. Some don't believe in borders. “But for the majority, it's just a sort of nice, lovely, cuddly idea of what Europe is. “It's changed, it isn't, it's failing, it's falling behind, and by the way, to join would cost us £42billion a year. £42billion a year would be our gross contribution.” Get the latest politics news straight to your phone Join us on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. You can check out at any time. Read our Privacy Policy Mr Burnham has opened the door to rejoining the bloc. But the Reform UK leader warned “it is very different” to the European Union Britain left. He said: “These bonkers economists saying ‘if we hadn't left the European Union, our GDP would be 6% up, 8%’ … What they're saying is if we hadn't left the single market, we'd be one of the richest countries in the world. “It's nonsense. We've massively outperformed France, Italy and Germany in terms of growth. “Ours is nothing to write home about. Our services exports to Europe are up 28% since Brexit. Is it more difficult to buy and sell physical goods? “Yes, it is, and that deal might – should be made easier. But at the same time, we've done 70 trade agreements around the rest of the world. And he is sticking to a completely outdated view.” Former Home Secretary Dame Priti Patel said: “Burnham is deluded to think the EU will provide Britain with a big economic boost when he has failed to be honest with the public about the enormous trade offs for UK taxpayers his EU reset will create. “From more mobility and free movement schemes, to concessions on fishing, farming and removing Britain’s ability to undertake free trade outside the EU and the inevitable price for joining EU schemes, this will be wrong for our country and will only cause further uncertainly and division. Our focus must be on building stronger Britain, investing in our country and people so we are less dependant upon others in this highly contested world." A Number 10 spokesman said: “The threadbare Brexit deal inherited by this Government has weakened our ability to control illegal immigration, slowed growth and left businesses tangled in red tape. We are working on practical deals that pay off for British farmers and families and will support growth in every UK postcode, cutting back on paperwork and easing pressure on prices.”
